terms.gloss: look around in case something’s coming
terms.grammar: imperative of circumspiciō, with nē and the present subjunctive
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 955: Circumspice dum, nē quis nostrō hīc auceps sermōnī siet.
Plaut. Trin. 146–147: Circumspicedum tē, nē quis adsit arbiter nōbīs, et quaesō identidem circumspice.
terms.comment: A sentence of ours, on the pattern of Plautus’s circumspice, nē quis …, said by someone making sure that nobody is coming. We have found no set phrase for looking both ways in the authors we searched or in Traupman.

terms.gloss: look to the right and to the left
evidence: Hor. S. 2.3.50: ille sinistrōrsum, hic dextrōrsum abit
terms.comment: A description of ours; Horace pairs the two adverbs of two men going wrong in a wood.

phrases.english: Look both ways first, then we’ll cross.

phrases.latin: Circumspicedum, numquis est sermōnem nostrum quī aucupet? — Tūtum probēst. — Circumspice etiam. — Nēmō est.
phrases.english: Have a look round: is anyone there to catch what we say? — It’s perfectly safe. — Look round again. — There’s nobody.

sources: Lewis & Short: circumspicio · Lewis & Short: dextrorsum
